item.title: Embattled Federal Employees Look to a Democratic Congress for a Lifeline
item.description:
Since the start of his second term, President Trump has gone after the federal work force, shearing 17 percent of employees, stripping away centuries of experience in medicine, law and science, and politicizing jobs meant to be nonpartisan.

Embattled current and former workers are now looking to Democrats, newly empowered after the Republican rout in the midterm elections, for help.

But the sweeping Democratic victories came with competing ideas for change, starting with issues like affordability, health care and the war in Iran. That could mean that any reversal of Mr. Trump’s cuts may have to wait.

Then there is the reality that a Democratic-led Congress is only going to be able to do so much while Mr. Trump is still in the White House.

“We’re playing a long game here while we’re trying to prevent and undo as much damage as possible in the short term,” said Representative James Walkinshaw, a Democrat from a Northern Virginia district that is home to many current and former federal workers. Mr. Walkinshaw, who helped create the Congressional Federal Workforce Caucus earlier this year, said he expected the Trump administration to continue its attacks on the federal work force.

“But now we have some constitutional and legal authority to push back,” he said.

Current and former federal workers have been waiting 20 months for this moment. More than 389,000 employees left the government last year, a mix of people who were fired or pressured to leave, according to government data. The Agriculture, Health and Human Services, Interior and Treasury Departments suffered some of the biggest hits.

The White House has defended Mr. Trump’s cuts, and has said that the government is leaner and more efficient, an argument that former and current workers dispute. They point to widespread chaos and vacancies that have left basic work, such as getting grants out the door, delayed.

Their wish list for the incoming Congress is long.

Some want Congress to reconstitute the U.S. Agency for International Development and improve how it handles humanitarian and foreign assistance. They want their collective bargaining rights returned. They also want help burnishing the reputation of the federal work force after the Trump administration cast it as full of do-nothing bureaucrats.

Some current and former federal workers most want accountability, including congressional hearings that would force Trump administration officials to explain why they rescinded funds allocated by Congress, conducted widespread layoffs, and canceled contracts and grants.

“A lot of this will take a long time,” said Aryn Melton Backus, a co-founder of the National Public Health Coalition, a nonprofit group composed of fired and laid off members of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. She spoke in her personal capacity and not for the C.D.C., as she is still on paid administrative leave.

Ms. Melton Backus said that a Democratic majority in Congress still offered more hope to whistle-blowers, because lawmakers could hold hearings and call witnesses.

“Part of the attitude over the past year and a half,” she said, “is people have been like, ‘Well, if I do blow the whistle, nothing’s going to happen. So then, I’m risking my career for, you know, something potentially not happening.’”

Across the federal diaspora, there is a sense of guarded optimism.

“They feel like there is a real hope, you know, because these last 20 months have been very devastating for them,” said Everett Kelley, the national president of the American Federation of Government Employees, the largest labor union for federal workers. “Just the mere fact that they feel like somebody that is going to at least stand up to the corruption, stand up to the bullying, and, you know, the dismantling of the government. They feel good about that.”

Agan Smalley, the president of Local 777 of the International Federation of Professional and Technical Engineers and a geologist in the Army Corps of Engineers, said she was looking forward to her union’s annual legislative conference in Washington in February, after two years of being ignored by many Republicans. The conference provides opportunities for workers to speak directly with lawmakers and their staff members about policies and workers’ rights.

“Some of the way things are supposed to be done will be happening again,” she said.

Sarah Kobrin, an employee at the National Institutes of Health, said that she was happy with the midterm elections results, but that the deep cuts to medical research and grant funding had been so vast that it would take much more than federal dollars to recoup the losses.

“It was a big battle to win. But it is far from winning the war,” she said, speaking in her personal capacity and not for the agency. Part of winning the war, she said, was limiting the authority Mr. Trump had given to Russell T. Vought, the director of the Office of Management and Budget and the architect of the most consequential measures to dismantle the federal government.

The breadth of repairs to the government that will be needed is clear to Zach Dembo, a first-time Democratic candidate who flipped a House district in Kentucky that had been held by a Republican since 2013. Mr. Dembo, who served in the Navy and left his job as a federal prosecutor in 2025, is among several incoming lawmakers who are former federal workers.

Mr. Dembo said he saw the administration’s efforts to politicize the government as a part of the corruption that many voters had complained of during his campaign.

“We’re all committed to a federal government that operates free of politicization,” Mr. Dembo said. “I think a lot of us never would have ran. We wanted to stay being feds if it weren’t for all the nonsense going on.”

item.title: Duffy Offers New Details on How One Fix Spiraled Into Nationwide Ground Stop
item.description:
The cascade of failures that led to the grounding of U.S. air traffic on Friday began with what officials say was supposed to be a routine router upgrade at a radio facility in El Dorado, Ark. The station was remote enough, they figured, that they could do the work without causing undue harm.

But that swiftly proved to be a gross miscalculation.

The effort to upgrade the Federal Aviation Administration’s antiquated copper-wire-based system to fiber optic cable in Arkansas occurred as the agency officials noticed a second issue with a radar facility in Amarillo, Texas, where such work had been done weeks before, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Sunday morning during a blitz of appearances across network and cable television.

Officials took the two facilities offline shortly after, but not before each had pinged the network with an abnormally high rate of connections. That prompted failures in other parts of the air traffic communications network that forced officials to declare a rare nationwide ground stop, Rebecca Guy, the F.A.A.’s chief technology officer, told reporters on Saturday.

But agency investigators still have not determined whether a faulty part or an error on the part of L3Harris, which owns the telecoms system in question and is responsible for upgrading and maintaining it, caused the initial problem in Arkansas. And Mr. Duffy said they are equally unsure why the facility in Amarillo failed on Friday when no upgrade work was being done there at the time.

The protracted crisis, from which airlines have yet to recover, and the lack of clarity from Trump administration officials about why things went wrong, have revived questions about whether the F.A.A. is equipped to carry out its plan for modernization without creating more risks for the nation’s air traffic control system.

The crisis has also heightened concerns about durability and the lack of backups in the nation’s critical air traffic infrastructure, if a failure at one small facility is enough to bring the functionality of the entire network down.

During an interview Sunday on NBC’s “Meet the Press,” Mr. Duffy said he could not guarantee that a meltdown like Friday’s would not happen again.

“First we have to figure out what happened,” he said, adding, “We’re going to figure out what was the root cause and then move forward from there, fixing how we do business at the F.A.A.”

He also deflected when asked if he was ultimately responsible for the meltdown and owed air passengers an apology.

“I can’t apologize for what was passed on to us,” he said, accusing prior administrations of having failed to tackle known infrastructure problems.

“I don’t apologize for shutting down the airspace and keeping people safe,” he added.

Skepticism surrounding how the F.A.A. has been carrying out its air traffic modernization plan is not new.

In September, the Government Accountability Office, a nonpartisan watchdog agency, issued a report raising concerns that the F.A.A. was in danger of “prioritizing speed over costs and air traffic disruptions” as it pursued its modernization plan. The report also criticized the agency for not having coordinated the schedules of 11,389 upgrade projects and not having conducted life-cycle cost estimates of existing technology, noting that “without them, the agency could end up causing air traffic disruptions or prolonging reliance on severely outdated systems.”

But such questions are especially pertinent since Mr. Duffy chose to seize on Friday’s meltdown by demanding that Congress give him $50 billion in new funding for air traffic control upgrades by the end of the year. That is a drastically larger sum than he has asked for before — and one that many lawmakers say he has not shown he would responsibly spend.

“It’s really rich to hear the secretary pointing the fingers at Congress when Congress has given the administration what they asked for,” Senator Chris Van Hollen, a Maryland Democrat running to become majority leader, said on CNN’s “State of the Union.” “If they need more, they should come up and justify it.”

On Saturday, the White House put its weight behind Mr. Duffy’s ballooning demand for funding, and on Sunday, President Trump weighed in on social media to claim that his administration could build the “BEST SYSTEM anywhere in the world,” urging Congress “to give the money, FAST!”

But Mr. Trump dedicated more of his attention to blasting the Biden administration for the F.A.A.’s air traffic infrastructure problems than detailing what $50 billion more would pay for.

Mr. Duffy also has yet to itemize his $50 billion request. For several weeks, he has been calling for a $30 billion influx in F.A.A. funding, but only about $10 billion of that request was specifically for air traffic modernization. Another $10 billion of the funds was envisioned for airport beautification, and the last $10 billion for improvement projects at towers, terminals and airports.

Last year, Congress appropriated $12.5 billion for air traffic modernization, nearly two-thirds of which lawmakers dedicated for telecoms upgrades and radar replacements.

On Saturday, Bryan Bedford, the F.A.A. administrator, told reporters that his agency would need “about $10.1 billion to finish modernization,” on top of the $12.5 billion Congress already appropriated.

On Sunday, Mr. Duffy said that while the money his department has requested will go to pay for needed radio and radar upgrades, it will not cover all the costs of upgrading a telecom system reliant in some places on 1980s wiring and routers from 2001 that have long been obsolete.

“What I don’t have money for is the new telecoms system; I don’t have money for new software,” Mr. Duffy said on CBS’s “Face the Nation.” “Those are critical pieces to the new infrastructure and it’s been historically underinvested in.”

item.title: Van Hollen Says His Senate Challenge to Schumer Is Gaining Support
item.description:
Senator Chris Van Hollen, a Maryland Democrat, contended on Sunday that he has a “wide open” path to unseat Senator Chuck Schumer of New York to become majority leader next year, intensifying the internal leadership battle that is dividing the newly empowered Democratic caucus.

Mr. Van Hollen, who has positioned himself as a populist underdog, said he did not believe Mr. Schumer’s support was solid. Mr. Schumer, an architect and funder of the successful Democratic effort to retake the Senate, has announced that he has locked up enough commitments to return him to the position of leader for another two years.

“I can tell you that a number of those people on that list have actually committed to voting for me,” Mr. Van Hollen said on CNN’s “State Of The Union,” though it was not clear what list he was referring to. “The others are very open to the idea of change.”

Mr. Van Hollen had previously said he had more than 10 colleagues supporting him.

On Sunday, he said on “Fox News Sunday” that number was up to 15 and growing. “This is a wide-open race,” he said.

The winner needs a simple majority of the caucus to vote for him in a secret-ballot election that is scheduled for Dec. 1. Democrats will make up at least 55 seats in the Senate next year, including the independents who caucus with them.

Mr. Van Hollen, 67, also accused Mr. Schumer, 75, who has led Senate Democrats since 2016, of trying to change that date because he was not confident he had the votes.

“If they really believed that they were ahead, they wouldn’t be trying to move up the elections,” Mr. Van Hollen, who appeared on three different programs on Sunday morning, said on Fox News. “They’re talking about trying to short-circuit that open debate process within the Democratic caucus.”

While there has been an internal discussion by some lawmakers of moving up the date of the election to avoid a prolonged internal battle, it is not clear that the idea has gained any traction and is not being driven by Mr. Schumer himself, people familiar with the conversations said.

Mr. Van Hollen said that he differed from Mr. Schumer in his position on funding the war with Iran. He said Congress should give “not one penny more” to fund the war, using the leverage of a government shutdown next month to force the issue. Congress has a Dec. 11 deadline to fund the government to avoid a shutdown.

Mr. Schumer and other top Democrats have been weighing a temporary extension of government funding with some restrictions on the military money until early 2027, when they would hold the majority and likely be able to exert more leverage against the Trump administration.

Mr. Van Hollen also said he disagreed with Mr. Schumer’s decision to try to influence Democratic primaries during the midterm elections, particularly against Senators-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan and Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota.

“He joined with AIPAC and crypto to try and defeat them,” he said, referring to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, which spent about $30 million in the competitive Michigan primary against Mr. El-Sayed.

While Mr. Schumer has been criticized for supporting some center-leaning candidates in primaries who ultimately lost to progressives, his allies noted that he recruited five winning candidates in states that Democrats flipped or are on track to do so: Mary Peltola in Alaska, Roy Cooper in North Carolina, Josh Turek in Iowa, Sherrod Brown in Ohio and Scott Colom in Mississippi.

They also noted that Senate Democrats’ campaign arm never spent money in the Minnesota Senate race.

Overall, though, Mr. Van Hollen said he was challenging Mr. Schumer because the message of the midterm elections was that the American people wanted change.

“We need to earn people’s trust, and I don’t think you do that by simply going back to business as usual,” Mr. Van Hollen said on Fox News.

item.title: Flight Delays and Cancellations Persist as Air Traffic System Recovers
item.description:
Air traffic operations over the United States continued to improve on Sunday after nearly all flights were grounded for more than 4 hours on Friday. Still, disruptions remained across the system with many flights canceled or delayed.

Nearly 90 percent of all flights left within 14 minutes of their scheduled departure time on Sunday morning, according to Cirium, an aviation analytics company. But some 5 percent of flights — more than 1,300 trips — had already been canceled, higher than a typical day, showing the continuing effects of the nationwide flight freeze.

Disruptions have occurred at major hubs — from Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport in Georgia to Dallas Fort Worth International Airport in Texas — and at airports in Phoenix and Philadelphia.

The disruptions postponed college sports games and stranded professional basketball teams. Passengers slept overnight in airports and competed to rebook their flights; some canceled their trips entirely.

The logjam is the latest example of the vulnerabilities in the American air traffic system, which is facing twin crises: a shortage of air traffic controllers and an outdated infrastructure.

It was an upgrade to the system that officials have identified as the root cause of the problems that led to the shutdown on Friday. As the contractor L3 Harris was upgrading copper wires to fiber-optic cables, a router overloaded the system with data requests, disrupting communications.

As a result, tens of thousands of passengers endured a nightmare travel weekend. Some 9,000 flights were canceled on Friday, according to Cirium, while about 30 percent were delayed. As airlines worked to get back on track on Saturday, there were still 6,649 cancellations and more than half of all flights were delayed.

“Our air traffic control system is operating on DECADES-OLD, analog equipment that simply cannot compete with the demands of the 21st century,” Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary, wrote on social media.

Officials said Sunday that they expected schedules to return to normal by late in the day or Monday morning.

For Ashley Greiner, 45, the delays have compounded.

On Saturday, her flight from Seattle to Atlanta was rerouted to Charlotte, N.C. But her connection to Atlanta was canceled, and she spent the night in North Carolina. On Sunday, she faced two delays and a plane change.

“I’m a heart-failure patient, and my trips were for speaking engagements to share my story with health care providers,” she said in a direct-message conversation. “This has been exceptionally hard on my body.”

The disruption in the communication system forced officials at the Federal Aviation Administration to ground flights at around 4 p.m. on Friday.

It was the third such ground stop this century.

Some 3,500 planes were airborne when the order went out, Secretary Duffy said on Friday.

Overall, more than 17,000 flights have been canceled since Friday, according to Cirium’s latest tally. Nearly 40 percent of the 74,696 scheduled flights since Friday have been delayed.

On Sunday, Secretary Duffy said the affected facilities in Texas and Arkansas were “secured” and diagnostic testing was underway.

“We have no indication of a foreign cyberattack, and we will continue to investigate alongside the F.B.I. and our federal law enforcement partners,” he said.

Brenda Folkerts, 59, arrived in New Orleans on Thursday for a marathon but now faces the prospect of a long trip to her home state of Washington on sore and tired legs. Her connection through Dallas was delayed by two hours on Sunday, and she missed her flight to Seattle. She does not know when or how she’ll make it home.

“My case is not unique,” she said in a direct message as her plane taxied. “Most people here have missed connections and are scrambling to figure out what to do.”

item.title: 8 Takeaways From a Big Democratic Gathering in Denver: Democrats in Array
item.description:
Democratic spirits were higher than the altitude in Denver, where more than 3,000 party strategists, activists, lawmakers and potential presidential candidates gathered last week to strategize how the party could capitalize on its dominant showing in the midterm elections.

Democrats flipped at least eight Senate seats while also securing what could be the largest House majority in a national election for either party in three decades.

“America is back,” Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the speaker-in-waiting, beamed at one welcome party.

For a party that is often fractious, there seemed little discord in Denver. Some of the loudest jeering over the three-day event came when the lights at the Ritz-Carlton hotel bar brightened and hundreds of drinking Democrats booed in unison at the thought of it closing.

Here are eight takeaways from the gathering.

More than a half-dozen potential Democratic presidential candidates descended on Denver to make early pitches for themselves and their visions. They were not technically campaigning — at least not yet. But they were all eager to share how much they had to give to the country.

At one point on Friday, Gov. Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania was speaking on the main stage while Senator Elissa Slotkin of Michigan was taking questions from reporters. Senator Ruben Gallego of Arizona was nearby, too, waiting to speak to the media.

Later, Senator Raphael Warnock of Georgia gave a speech, then stayed to listen to Senator Cory Booker of New Jersey address the crowd. And Pete Buttigieg, the former transportation secretary, was sought after — especially after a rare nationwide ground stop was issued.

The pileup of hopefuls previewed what could be a crowded campaign.

The conference was hosted by Majority Democrats, a relatively new group that espouses a less ideological brand of Democratic politics and focuses on recruiting younger candidates. The group is funded chiefly by the hedge-fund billionaire Stephen Mandel and his wife, Sue. But billionaires still found themselves in the cross hairs of some progressives.

Representative Ro Khanna of California, who is considering a presidential run, called for a wealth tax on billionaires and accused Israel of a genocide to cheers.

Since Mr. Shapiro has rarely left Pennsylvania this year, his presence alone in Denver was notable. But on Friday, he spoke about his ambitions for the party — and his role in its future — both in his speech and an interview. He called it imperative for Democrats to construct a party that could win “370 electoral votes” — not just the 270 needed to win the presidency.

“We can’t be a party that is focused on sloganeering,” Mr. Shapiro said in an interview. “We have to be a party that’s focused on real deliverables.”

He said that the party can’t become “distracted by the shallow litmus test or trying to figure out where someone fits on some imaginary political spectrum.”

For many years, the Democratic presidential primary began in Iowa and New Hampshire, and then went to South Carolina. No longer.

In 2028, six early states will open the primary calendar: South Carolina, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Mexico, Michigan and Virginia.

Officials in Michigan, Virginia and New Mexico are already plotting how to take advantage of the new attention, circulating among ambitious Democrats on the sidelines of the conference.

For instance, Mr. Buttigieg ate Friday night with Don Scott, the House speaker in Virginia, which will hold the final primary before Super Tuesday. Mr. Scott said he told Mr. Buttigieg to start meeting with local leaders now if he wanted to be competitive in Virginia.

Shapiro. Gallego. Warnock. Booker. Khanna. Buttigieg.

Gov. JB Pritzker of Illinois had aides and advisers circulating in Denver. So did Gov. Andy Beshear of Kentucky and Gov. Wes Moore of Maryland.

All those potential 2028 candidates — as well as Gov. Gavin Newsom of California, who was attending a climate summit in Turkey — are men.

Although women seem less certain to run, some could chase the Democratic nomination. That group includes former Vice President Kamala Harris, Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York and Ms. Slotkin, who gave the clearest indications yet that she was considering a run, saying in an interview that she was “seriously” weighing a bid.

Although she said that gender was not reason alone to run for the nation’s highest office, she added it was hard to ignore the possibility of the party being represented by only men in the primary.

“I would hate to see us go backwards by having no women enter the fray,” she said. Later, she said, “I know I want to be a part of the next generation that is helping to lead. That doesn’t necessarily mean I have to be the top dog.”

Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland arrived in Denver a day after declaring his underdog candidacy to unseat Senator Chuck Schumer of New York as the top Democrat in the Senate.

He received loud cheers when he restated his intention to the crowd, but Mr. Van Hollen is unlikely to succeed. One conference attendee came wearing a “Van Hollen For Leader” shirt modeled after the Van Halen logo but did not want to discuss on the record his support for the Maryland Democrat.

Mr. Van Hollen is an unlikely avatar of trying to upend the political status quo. He told reporters that he had “a record of running against the establishment,” while also noting in the same answer that he had served as chairman of both the House Democratic campaign arm and the Senate Democratic campaign arm.

“What has never changed about me is that I still believe we can support the underdog,” Mr. Van Hollen said.

In a small sign of frustration with the party’s old guard, Mr. Jeffries was repeatedly heckled while speaking onstage with Jessica Tarlov, a co-host of Fox News’s “The Five.” Mr. Jeffries waved off the hecklers dismissively by noting he was from Brooklyn.

“They didn’t win over a single person, but at least they got their clips for social,” Ms. Tarlov said afterward.

Ms. Slotkin said one of the most important qualities for a candidate in this media landscape was simply being compelling.

“The way citizens consume presidential elections is fundamentally changing,” she said. “I’m not sure we’ll ever have a boring president ever again.”

She just watched Abdul El-Sayed, a charismatic progressive, succeed in Michigan. And after a cycle in which a deluge of Republican cash failed to yield much return on the party’s investments, Democrats debated on the sidelines whether paid ads were as important as earning organic attention and riding the algorithm of social media.

“You can have all the great policy papers you want,” Ms. Slotkin said. “If you can’t convey authentically, that’s going to hold you back. And I think that’s actually OK.”

There was broad agreement among the could-be presidential candidates — and the Democrats who might work for them — that the time for choosing was near.

The competition for attention, donors and top staff is already steep. Many Democrats in Denver spoke of the relative dearth of top operatives who were eager to dedicate themselves to the rigors of a presidential primary campaign — especially with so many new Democratic congressional offices also staffing up.

Mr. Shapiro said he might announce his decision even before he tried to enact a robust agenda in the first 100 days with new Democratic state legislative majorities. Ms. Slotkin said she would decide early next year. And Mr. Warnock, who may have to choose between running for president and seeking Senate re-election in 2028, said nobody could dawdle.

“I don’t think there’s much time for anybody who thinks they want to do this,” he said.

item.title: Nvidia Fallout Looms Over Trump-Xi Meeting
item.description:
At major moments in President Trump’s second term, he has looked up during an economic speech or diplomatic dinner and asked a version of the same question: “Where’s Jensen?”

Jensen Huang has usually been out there, somewhere in the room.

Mr. Huang, who was until Thursday the leather-jacketed chief executive of Nvidia, one of the world’s largest companies, had impressed the president with his success, his money and his argument that keeping China dependent on American-made semiconductor chips and technology could help maintain U.S. dominance over Beijing.

Mr. Trump made sure to have the technology executive with him during pivotal U.S.-China meetings this year. The president invited him to come to China in May when he went to meet with Xi Jinping, China’s leader, stopping in Alaska, where Mr. Huang joined him on Air Force One at the last minute. And Mr. Huang was at the head table with the president when Mr. Trump hosted a state dinner for Mr. Xi at the White House in September.

But when Mr. Trump travels to China for another meeting with Mr. Xi at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation in Shenzhen this week, Mr. Huang, the man who has been influential in shaping the president’s views about technological competition with China, is not expected to be at his side.

Last week, Mr. Huang stepped down from his role at Nvidia after revelations that he had engaged in affairs, including one with Alice Huang, a woman who U.S. intelligence officials believe is an asset of Beijing.

Mr. Huang’s sudden fall and the U.S. finding that he was targeted by Chinese intelligence do not appear to have altered Mr. Trump’s estimation of the former Nvidia leader — or his approach to dealing with his Chinese counterpart in this week’s meeting. (Beijing has called the U.S. intelligence conclusions “smears and slanders.”)

So far, the president has not pressed Mr. Xi about his country’s espionage efforts or stepped in to resolve a raging debate within his administration about tightening export controls of A.I. technology and certain chips to China. Howard Lutnick, the commerce secretary, who has argued for less strict limits on chip exports to Asia, is expected to travel with him. In Shenzhen, Mr. Trump will participate in a meeting with Mr. Xi and, later, with Mr. Xi and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia, in the first such gathering of the three leaders.

“Well, the big thing is, was the woman a spy?” Mr. Trump said in an interview with the podcaster and sports commentator Stephen A. Smith on Thursday, when asked if he thought Mr. Huang should have resigned. “And I don’t know if that’s been determined yet, but if the woman was a spy, yes. If the woman was not a spy, perhaps it would be different. But I can tell you this: Somehow, he’ll end up in his feet. I mean, I know him. I know him pretty well. I always thought of him as a fine man.”

Mr. Trump said last week that he did not plan to bring up the Nvidia matter with Mr. Xi but suggested that the Chinese leader could bring it up with him.

The president also said that he did not recall being briefed that Mr. Huang was in a close relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese executive believed by the United States to be a Chinese intelligence asset.

But Secretary of State Marco Rubio told Mr. Trump aboard Air Force One in May en route to China about the sensitive intelligence showing that Nvidia’s chief executive was in a relationship with the woman and that she was believed to be a Chinese spy, The New York Times reported last week. It was at least the second time the president was briefed on the intelligence, The Times reported.

Mr. Trump has continued to defend Mr. Huang, calling him an “honorable man” and questioning reports that he was briefed on the government’s intelligence findings.

“I’d have to check,” he told reporters last week in response to a question about when he first learned of the matter. “I’d certainly check with the intelligence people. They could have been mentioned. Certainly, it didn’t make much of an impact on me.”

The president’s blasé response to espionage allegations that have upended one of the world’s largest companies belies the economic and political storm caused by the revelations of Mr. Huang’s behavior. It also raises questions about how Mr. Trump would conduct himself during his meeting with Mr. Xi, an authoritarian leader whose friendship and admiration the president has courted.

“Trump has stood by Huang personally, and my read is that he sees espionage as something major powers just do to each other,” Craig Singleton, a China expert at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a nonpartisan think tank, said during a briefing last week. “He wants a very successful meeting and to show that he can manage the relationship with Xi Jinping.”

Indeed, Mr. Trump has said that espionage is the price of dealing with a powerful adversary. “You know what they say? That China spies on us. I say you’re right, and we spy on them, too,” he said in September.

White House officials said Friday that the Nvidia matter was a national security issue, and they did not expect the president to discuss it with Mr. Xi during their encounter.

In his two previous meetings this year with the Chinese leader, Mr. Trump showed little interest in extracting concessions from China.

Mr. Trump struck a conciliatory tone with Mr. Xi during his visit to Beijing in May, emphasizing their personal relationship. And when Mr. Xi visited Washington in the fall, weeks after Mr. Trump decried what he claimed was meddling by Beijing in the 2020 election, the president leaned into the pageantry of the occasion. The state visit produced little in terms of policy announcements on matters of tension between the two countries — on A.I., trade or the war in Iran.

But as Mr. Trump prepares to head to China again, Mr. Singleton noted that “the politics back in Washington are moving in a very different direction.”

The Trump administration is now facing questions and criticism over whether officials had properly policed the sale of chips to China. On Friday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent publicly blamed the Commerce Department for failing to curb the sale of advanced Nvidia technology to the Singaporean firm Megaspeed, which employed Ms. Huang and built data centers that provide computing power to Chinese companies.

“You will have to ask them about their internal processes,” he said of the Commerce Department, adding that his own agency had supported a stricter approach. “Treasury and my deputy has been pushing for this for months at the deputies level.”

Mr. Bessent has led the administration’s efforts to extend a trade truce with Beijing that expires in January. Despite continuing negotiations and the pause of a tit-for-tat trade war, administration officials remain frustrated with China’s restrictions on exports of crucial rare-earth metals and rare-earth magnets. Mr. Trump is expected to bring up that issue with Mr. Xi in Shenzhen.

While administration officials say the president will focus his meetings on rare-earth exports, nuclear proliferation and the war with Iran, Republicans and Democrats in Washington are demanding answers on Nvidia from Mr. Huang and Mr. Lutnick, who both have been asked to testify before the Senate Banking Committee in December.

“If Beijing was trying to keep American chips flowing, it may have helped build the bipartisan case for cutting that access off,” Mr. Singleton said.

It remains to be seen if that political pressure will force Mr. Trump to impose new restrictions on technology exports, or make another move that could constrain China.

Kenton Thibaut, a senior resident China fellow at the Atlantic Council, said that the Nvidia scandal was a “miserable” scenario for the Chinese, whose diplomatic aim with Mr. Trump is to placate him and keep a competitive relationship steady while reducing dependence on the economic choke points that Americans control.

“They wanted to keep this stasis in U.S.-China relations, prevent sort of any more export controls from coming into place, play nice with Trump and not rock the boat in any way,” Ms. Thibaut said. “And this is kind of like a disaster for them.”

]]>

item.title: How Could a Router Lead to a Nationwide Ground Stop?
item.description:
Thousands of flights were halted for hours on Friday after officials issued a rare nationwide ground stop, creating a cascade of delays and cancellations that continued over the weekend.

Government officials blamed the disarray on a router in Arkansas that sent a flood of data into the Federal Aviation Administration’s system after an upgrade. Workers also noticed a second unspecified issue at another complex in Texas.

Officials shut down the airspace out of an abundance of caution as the network became “unpredictable and unreliable,” said Michael McCormick, a professor at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University in Daytona Beach, Fla.

“It was a smart decision to actually decide to ground-stop all air departures,” he said.

On Sunday, authorities were still working to determine an exact cause for the communications network failure that prompted officials to issue the ground stop.

Here’s what we know about what could have caused the domino effect at airports.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on Sunday that the cascade of failures began during a routine router upgrade at a radio facility in El Dorado, Ark. Workers felt that the station was remote enough to work on without causing undue harm, which turned out not to be the case.

Across the country, the Federal Aviation Administration has slowly been modernizing its antiquated copper-wire-based system to fiber optic cable, which was what workers were upgrading in Arkansas at the time of the network crash.

Agency officials also noticed a second unspecified issue at a radar facility in Amarillo, Texas, that had been upgraded weeks before.

Officials took the two facilities offline shortly afterward, but each had already pinged the communications network hundreds of times per second, overwhelming an antiquated system. That prompted failures in other parts of the air traffic communications network, prompting officials to issue the ground stop.

The F.A.A. uses tens of thousands of routers to operate its communications network. Those routers, called switches, are typically larger and industrial grade, designed to withstand harsh environments, Mr. McCormick said.

The routers used by the F.A.A. were made by Cisco Systems and Juniper Networks, a company purchased by Hewlett Packard Enterprise last year. The agency said it had been gradually replacing older Cisco routers with newer Juniper ones.

The routers in the F.A.A.’s communications system process much more data than the household internet routers that many Americans are familiar with. The government routers run on a closed, private network to prevent cyberattacks, and they have to be able to interpret and process radar data, flight plans and audio and transmit the information to the right places.

Aviation experts said it was likely that when the new router came online in Arkansas, the device began to send so much information that it overwhelmed the older equipment, which could not respond fast enough. That led to a cascade of issues.

“Now you have multiple parts of the old system that are running much faster than they ever ran,” said R. John Hansman, a professor of aeronautics and astronautics at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. “You never had this problem, because you never had all of the elements running at that max speed.”

Friday’s crisis has raised concerns about the durability and the lack of backups in the nation’s air traffic infrastructure, since a failure at one small facility was enough to bring down the entire network.

“The idea that you would have a single router take down a national network is just not plausible,” said Robert W. Mann Jr., who founded an airline analysis and consulting firm. He expressed skepticism about the Transportation Department’s explanation.

He added, “What we really have here is a demonstration that what we knew a decade ago was problematic done at small scale is really, really problematic done at nationwide scale.”

Mr. Duffy and other government officials were quick to blame the country’s aging air traffic system for the breakdown, arguing that Congress needed to allot more funding for urgently needed updates.

They also pointed fingers at the F.A.A.’s contractor, L3Harris. L3Harris owns the telecommunications network and was performing the system upgrade, which also involved replacing old copper wiring with modern fiber optic cables.

Officials are still trying to determine if the communications failure was caused by a faulty part or an error on the part of the contractor.

L3Harris said in a statement that it was cooperating with the investigation.

Experts cautioned that rushing the upgrades to the decades-old system posed new risks, as the legacy communications network still needs to run while the new one is being installed and then thoroughly tested.

Perhaps, they suggested, the hardware and software changes could be done during a night shift rather than during peak flying hours.

Karoun Demirjian and Niraj Chokshi contributed reporting.

item.title: A Bull Market, Fueled by Pikachu, Charizard and Nostalgia
item.description:
Scott Pratte turned his boyhood hobby into his livelihood. But he doesn’t usually tell people he’s a Pokémon card collector.

In conversations, he is vague about what he does for a living, saying his business involves collectibles or investments.

“I wouldn’t want to share numbers on the record,” Mr. Pratte, 39, said in an interview, though he noted that the past few years have been “million-dollar years in earnings.”

Pokémon originated as a pair of video games released in Japan for Nintendo’s Game Boy console in 1996. The franchise expanded to include a trading card game, released the same year, which came to the United States in 1999. That’s when Mr. Pratte and others first marveled at the artwork, swapped cards on playgrounds and obsessed over completing sets they shrouded in plastic sleeves in protective binders.

As Pokémon has grown — on its 30th anniversary, the franchise now spans TV shows and films, all manner of merchandise and a stable of more than 1,000 “pocket monsters” — the cards have skyrocketed in value.

Logan Paul, a social media influencer and professional wrestler, sold a rare Pikachu Illustrator card from 1998 at an auction in February for a record $16.5 million. Rarity and nostalgia help drive prices, collectors say, as well as the grading of the cards by authentication companies.

“It is very similar to trading stocks,” Mr. Pratte said. “I think Pikachu and the cute little Pokémon on the cards distract from how competitive and cutthroat it can be.”

What started as a childhood hobby ballooned into a lucrative career because “I genuinely like them,” he said of the cards.

As their value increases, he finds it harder to associate the cards with the same magical memories of his youth — but he understands their enduring appeal.

“Certain cards have become so valuable that you have to sell them,” Mr. Pratte said. “We wouldn’t be able to sell cards for these prices if that emotional value didn’t exist.”

Gary Haase, known online as King Pokémon, was a middle-aged father when he started collecting as a way to bond with his sons. They enjoyed playing the card game and relished opening packs. One of the boys, he recalled, once fell asleep clutching a card featuring the hugely popular character Charizard.

When his children became teenagers and started finding girls more interesting than Pokémon, Mr. Haase kept up with the hobby. As a lifelong collector of sports cards and other items, he understood the value of keeping the cards in mint condition.

Guinness World Records recognizes him as owning the most valuable Pokémon card collection in the world. Part of Mr. Haase’s trove, including multiple rare Charizard cards, is listed on eBay for $59 million.

But he has no intention of actually selling. Ten years ago he put it up for $15 million to “just show it off so people can see it and enjoy it,” he said.

As Pokémon card values rise, he keeps the price at what he estimates to be $10 million to $20 million above market value. “I don’t want somebody to hit it and then I’m obligated to sell,” Mr. Haase said.

In Britain, another father of a Pokémon fan continued collecting in the early 2000s after his son outgrew the hobby. At some point, he put the collection in his attic and didn’t think much of it until he saw a local newspaper article about a Pokémon card that had sold at auction for £6,000, or about $8,000.

The man then took his collection to Ewbank’s Auctions in Surrey, a county southwest of London, which had sold the card. A conservative early estimate by the auction house — which said the man had requested anonymity — suggested that his cards could fetch several hundred thousand pounds, said Andrew Ewbank, a partner at Ewbank Auctions.

Leading up to the auction, it seemed as if the collection would top expectations, as interest spiked and people paid visits to inspect the cards while donning white gloves. The cards, auctioned off in sets, ended up selling for £1.5 million, or about $2.1 million, Mr. Ewbank said.

Lee Steinfeld quit his lawyer job in 2017 to be a full-time YouTube personality. As “Leonhart,” he has more than two million subscribers who tune into see him rip into packs with the same delight he had for the cards as a young boy.

“I’m absolutely grateful to be doing what I do, opening up Pokémon cards for a living,” said Mr. Steinfeld, 39, of Dallas. “I can’t believe I’m not tired of this.”

All markets are prone to fluctuation; in fact, The New York Times reported when the bottom fell out of Pokémon cards 25 years ago, at a time when a high of $375 for the rarest cards seems very affordable by current standards. But there are few signs of a slowdown today, when streamers such as Mr. Steinfeld are a common presence at card conventions and the boom in Pokémon cards drives up the broader trading card market.

Reece Felix, 25, an owner of Aloha Card Shop with stores across Hawaii, traces the success of his business to his childhood love for Pokémon. When he was growing up on the Big Island, his mother would take him to a Kmart store to buy cards when he earned good grades.

It’s become more socially acceptable for adults to collect Pokémon cards, he said in a phone interview from Japan, where he was opening another store.

In 2022, his first store in Honolulu was robbed at gunpoint of Pokémon and sports cards worth around $36,000 — a scary memory for Mr. Felix, but one that shows the high stakes involved in the hobby.

The joy that collecting Pokémon cards brings him outweighs his desire to sell them, he said: “I definitely know how to invest in Pokémon cards and I have done so successfully, but my collector brain outweighs my want-to-have-cash brain.”

Kian Golshan started in high school, learning how to turn cards into valuable assets. (He played Pokémon on his Game Boy when he was younger.)

Now, 27, he said he was intent on buying cards that he hoped would appreciate. And they have: One collection he bought in 2020 for about $8,000 is now worth about $200,000 to $300,000, he said.

“Based on all my research, I knew that this was a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to purchase it at the time,” said Mr. Golshan, who lives in Southern California. “It was in immaculate condition.”

The Pokémon cards are still mostly a hobby Mr. Golshan, who works in finance.

“It was a combination of a lot of luck and some research from a while ago that ended up paying off, but I would hope people don’t go into debt,” he said.

Rylie Avery is a Pokémon fan who prides herself on not spending a lot of money collecting the cards.

A 24-year-old kindergarten teacher in Jackson, Mich., Ms. Avery says one of her earliest childhood memories is crawling around her older brother’s bedroom and picking cards out of the floorboards. She has always been drawn to the artwork, and enjoys giving cards to students.

Everyday collectors are more driven by emotion than monetary value, she said.

“It’s something they love or find cute and adorable,” she said. “It brings them joy, not just from the money, but just from a love of the game.”

item.title: Democrats Will Wield Enormous Power in Statehouses. What Will They Do?
item.description:
The midterm tsunami that swept Democrats to power in Congress also gave them control of state capitals from Pennsylvania to Nevada where they will be able to wield power swiftly and consequentially, in ways that will impact lives almost immediately.

Democrats will control the governorship and both legislative houses in six new states — Arizona, Wisconsin, Pennsylvania, Nevada, Michigan and Minnesota — and hold the majority in a dozen new statehouse chambers.

At least 530 legislative seats changed parties across the country, the Democrats’ best showing since the Watergate era and the biggest partisan swing since Republicans gained more than 700 seats and flipped 22 chambers in 2010.

“It is hard to overstate how massive of a political earthquake this was,” said State Representative Oscar De Los Santos, the incoming Arizona House speaker, who at age 33, wasn’t even alive the last time Arizona Democrats held the majority in any legislative chamber.

What comes next could be dramatic.

In Wisconsin, Pennsylvania and Nevada, Democrats want to raise the minimum wage, strengthen unions and pass paid family leave. They will face minimal opposition from powerless Republicans in the minority.

In Georgia and Texas, where Democrats will unexpectedly occupy the governor’s office and control their state houses, Republicans still holding the state senates will face enormous pressure to finally expand Medicaid under the Affordable Care Act. Wisconsin, one of the few states outside the South that has not expanded Medicaid, could do so quickly.

New Democratic governors will also move to rein in data centers and artificial intelligence.

And in Arizona, Democrats who have not held control of the legislature and governor’s mansion in 60 years, are determined to repeal abortion restrictions and revamp a costly school vouchers program as part of what Mr. De Los Santos called “big, bold initiatives that help working people.”

In a nationalized political environment, media and voter attention have gravitated to the presidency and Congress. But checks, balances, vetoes and filibusters will continue to be the rule in Washington, where government remains divided, even if Democrats will enjoy larger congressional majorities than they’ve seen in years.

The action, instead, might be in the states, where power can be less checked by structure and tradition.

In all, 22 states will have Democratic “trifectas” — a Democratic governor and both chambers of the legislature. Alaska will have a functional trifecta, with the Democratic governor-elect, Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, working with a coalition of Democrats, Republicans and independents that he helped assemble.

Tension between centrists and a resurgent left wing are inevitable, but Democratic leaders expressed optimism that at least in the initial rush, they can find consensus.

“It’s just the legislative process,” said Austin Davis, the Pennsylvania lieutenant governor, “which I think will be a lot easier with members of the same party controlling all three branches of government.”

So Mr. De Los Santos said he was consulting with other states with recent experience in flipping chambers, such as Minnesota and Michigan, and ones with strong Democratic majorities, like next-door New Mexico.

Democratic legislators and organizers are also workshopping ideas and taking a page from the American Legislative Exchange Council, which has worked for decades with conservative lawmakers and business interests to draft model legislation.

“There’s just such a tremendous feeling of optimism and also urgency,” said Gaby Goldstein, the founder of State Futures, a network of 900 progressive lawmakers which has organized state officials to push back on President Trump’s mass deportations and other policies. “This is crunchtime between now and January for a lot of the agenda setting.”

The most closely watched new trifecta could be Wisconsin.

Governor-elect David Crowley, a moderate Democrat, will be flanked by a state House and Senate controlled by Democrats for the first time since 2010. At that time, the then-governor, Scott Walker, and his fellow Republicans moved quickly to strip public union bargaining rights; cut income taxes; reduce education funding; expand vouchers for private school tuition; and approve gerrymandered State House and Senate maps that would lock in their power for years.

Though Gov. Tony Evers, a Democrat, has served for two terms, he has mostly played goalie, using veto power and attempting to block legislation pushed by Republicans.

Democrats’ memories may well be long. Greta Neubauer, the incoming Assembly speaker, said in an interview this week that she and her Democratic colleagues intended to move quickly. Their initial aim, she said, will be addressing the cost of living by lowering the costs of groceries, gas, health care and child care.

That could mean a bill that expands access to free or reduced-price meals in schools, which would help families have lower grocery costs, or a tax credit for renters and homeowners that essentially lowers property taxes.

“We of course have many other priorities as well — protecting people’s rights and freedoms, strengthening our democracy, building strong schools and creating good jobs,” Ms. Neubauer said.

In an email, Mr. Walker said that the new Democratic leaders “have every right to enact their own agenda.”

But he warned that if they deviated from a focus on cost of living issues, another political backlash could be in store.

“If liberals ignore the will of the people,” he said, “there will be another major shift in the 2028 elections.”

Michigan might be more cautious, said Maggie Mick, a senior vice president at MultiState, a state and local government relations firm. That is in part, she said, because Democrats are cognizant of how they lost their trifecta in 2024 after swinging big on abortion, right-to-work and L.G.B.T.Q. issues.

“They have gone through the whiplash of losing the majority,” she said.

In Pennsylvania, where Democrats captured the State Senate for the first time since the 1990s, whatever Harrisburg does will be viewed through the lens of an anticipated 2028 presidential run by Gov. Josh Shapiro, a Democrat.

With a comfortable majority in the House and a slim one in the state senate, Democrats intend to quickly enact laws that would increase transit funding, more than double the minimum wage, expand the availability of housing, add amendments to the constitution protecting abortion rights and allowing people to seek civil damages for childhood sexual abuse.

Those five items, which Gov. Shapiro has championed, “hit a sweet spot,” said State Representative Mike Schlossberg, a Democrat. “They’re relatively easy to pass, they’re highly popular and they’re incredibly important.”

This list aligns with Mr. Shapiro’s brand as a center-left Democrat. Even if some lawmakers would want to push the agenda further to the left, there is not much room for dissension: the Democrats need every vote of their caucus in the State Senate to pass legislation.

But disagreements are inevitable, said State Senator Nikil Saval, a Democrat and a member of the Democratic Socialists of America.

“Those debates will engage a broad section of the public who felt shut out of politics in Harrisburg until now,” he said.

Beyond that initial list of priorities, some legislation may include bills about the regulation of gambling and marijuana.

Several states are also likely to tackle concerns about utility bills and data centers.

In Georgia, Democrats won the governor’s office and the state House of Representatives, as well as a majority for the first time in decades on the Georgia Public Service Commission, which regulates utilities.

State Senator Chuck Hufstetler, a Republican who chairs his chamber’s finance committee, wanted to create a consumer watchdog office and require that data centers pay more, only to be blocked by his own party’s leaders. He plans to introduce new bills in 2027.

“I do see a bipartisan path forward,” he texted last week, while on a trip to China with a U.S. delegation looking at utilities and energy infrastructure.

Curbing health care costs is likely to be a common denominator in many states. In an interview with The New York Times, Georgia’s governor-elect, Keisha Lance Bottoms, said she was already drafting a budget that assumes the state will expand Medicaid, bringing government-funded health insurance to more middle-class Georgians — if the narrowly controlled Republican Senate goes along.

Ms. Goldstein, of State Futures, anticipated a renewed push in several states to prohibit medical debt from being included in credit reports. States could also band together to purchase prescription drugs in bulk to reduce costs.

Another priority is abortion access, said Bella Pori, associate director of state policy for Reproductive Freedom for All.

She pointed to North Carolina, where Democrats will control the House and likely end up just shy of controlling the Senate. Over the last decade, Republicans have dramatically increased funding to crisis pregnancy centers, which critics say are anti-abortion fronts. Such centers receive more than $10 million a year in the state.

Next year, Democrats may propose that there be no funding or less funding.

She also pointed to Arizona, where Democrats are likely to enact a shield law protecting providers and out-of-state patients, and also to repeal abortion restrictions.

At a news conference Tuesday at the state capitol in Phoenix, Democratic leaders said they wanted to increase funding for public schools, which have been strained by a program supplying vouchers for private schools, often to Arizonans who already had their children in those schools. They also want to further protect Arizona’s dwindling supply of groundwater, said Priya Sundareshan, the State Senate’s president-elect.

“Our job now is to make sure that you feel the difference at your kitchen table, in your kids’ classrooms and in your community,” she said.

Gov. Katie Hobbs marveled at how, 15 years ago, as a member of state legislature, she had so few Democratic colleagues that they called themselves the One Pizza Caucus, because a single pie could feed them all.

“We’re going to need a lot more pizzas,” she said.

item.title: Raman Has Lots of Plans. Los Angeles Has Lots of Obstacles.
item.description:
A month before Nithya Raman swept to victory as Los Angeles’s next mayor, she announced what she would do in her first 100 days if she won.

The audience was scant — the speech had somehow been scheduled outside during the dinner hour on a Sunday in searing heat with the Dodgers at home in the playoffs. Still, her most ardent fans gathered, sweltering, around her. If they expected a fire-breathing leftist manifesto from their candidate, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, they were wrong.

Ms. Raman, a 45-year-old member of the Los Angeles City Council with a master’s degree in urban planning, didn’t talk about defunding police, removing the private sector from housing construction or other items from a D.S.A. wish list. Rather, she outlined a near future of mapping out trouble spots and restructuring org charts. She would launch dashboards and audits, she said, and base performance evaluations on results and metrics. In her pursuit of a more livable city, she would drill down to a “nitty-gritty” so granular that it would “make your eyes glaze over.”

“In just one century, Los Angeles built itself into a global metropolis, the gateway to the Pacific, a center of ingenuity and invention, and the cultural capital of the entire planet,” Ms. Raman exhorted. “Don’t tell me the city of Los Angeles can’t fix a streetlight!”

The speech was a striking shift in a deep-blue city that has spent the past decade consumed with big-picture crises: Covid-19. Natural disasters. Clashes with the Trump administration, particularly over federal immigration enforcement. In many ways, political experts say, the election Ms. Raman won two weeks ago was a plea for a way back to normal.

“The issue in this election was not left versus right, but change versus the same,” said Zev Yaroslavsky, the director of the Los Angeles Initiative at the University of California, Los Angeles, and a longtime civic leader. “It was broken versus fixed.”

What Ms. Raman will be able to “fix” in Los Angeles is an open question. Power to enact policy in the city is diffuse. The mayor represents only about 4 million of the 10 million residents of Los Angeles County. Local authority is shared not only with the 15-member City Council but also with the county Board of Supervisors, which controls most social service spending.

In two years, a shift in governance that voters approved in 2024 will turn the top county government job into an elective office, effectively installing a new, more powerful countywide leader to rival Ms. Raman.

The city’s budget — roughly $13 billion not counting the city’s water and power department and airport — has been stretched thin, in part by commitments made under Karen Bass, the current mayor. The police union, which heavily backed Ms. Bass for re-election, received significant raises during her tenure, constraining the amount of money that Ms. Raman will have for projects.

Downtown business interests, which backed Ms. Bass as well, won an overhaul of the city convention center that is projected to siphon more than $100 million annually from the city’s general fund in debt service for the next three decades. The Olympics, typically a huge financial risk for the host city, are coming to town in 2028.

In interviews, Ms. Raman’s supporters and local political experts predicted that she will draw from a new generation of Democratic big-city mayors to push her agenda. They include the democratic socialist Zohran Mamdani in New York, political centrists like Daniel Lurie in San Francisco and progressive technocrats like Michelle Wu in Boston.

Like Mr. Lurie, her advisers say, she intends to rebrand her embattled city as a comeback story. Like Mr. Mamdani, she plans to improve the housing supply and tenant protections. Like Ms. Wu, she is likely to rely heavily on data and community input. Like all three, they add, her approach is less likely to be ideological than pragmatic.

“There has been a wave in our way of thinking about mayors,” said Megan Mullin, a professor of public affairs at the University of California, Los Angeles. “A mayor can be a visionary, or a power broker, or a political boss, or a coalition builder. This is an idea of the mayor as the manager of a big operation that delivers services that make our lives possible in a city — the mayor as C.E.O.”

Historically, politics in sprawling Los Angeles have been driven by single-family homeowners who commute by freeway. But precinct-level data that has emerged in the vote for mayor shows that Ms. Raman was carried into office amid surging turnout by young voters and Latinos, who are more likely to rent and rely on public transit.

“A city that works” was her slogan, but rent control laws for tenants and dedicated lanes on the streets for bicycle enthusiasts and bus riders are not necessarily appealing to older property owners and freeway commuters, said Mike Bonin, executive director of the Pat Brown Institute for Public Affairs at Cal State Los Angeles.

“It’s a big shift, and it’s largely generationally driven,” Mr. Bonin said. “Where the two groups do coincide is just on this sense that the city is broken and let’s clean it up.”

Ms. Raman, 45, who joined the City Council six years ago in the aftermath of the George Floyd protests, has favored left-leaning policy goals like strong rent regulations, denser housing near public transit and a less militarized approach to policing. At the time, she was endorsed by the D.S.A., the movement that later would help elect Mr. Mamdani.

She has since had a fraught relationship with the organization. During her campaign, she vowed to regard it as just one part of her governing coalition, though the movement clearly influenced her pledge to replace the police chief.

Ms. Raman has said she will reorganize lines of authority in the mayor’s office, designating a “chief operating officer” and a “chief financial officer” to help her manage the dozens of department heads in the city who answer to the mayor but, in practice, have often operated with scant oversight.

She also has promised to appoint a “recovery czar” for Pacific Palisades, where rebuilding from the 2025 wildfires has been sluggish; a “nightlife czar” to revive the city’s restaurant scene and cultural districts; a Hollywood liaison to speed permitting and market local production; an advocate for renters to run an “office of tenant protections”; and an “experienced financial executive” to oversee city spending on the 2028 Olympics, which could cost Los Angeles hundreds of millions of dollars if there are overruns.

In concert with the city controller, Kenneth Mejia, a D.S.A.-aligned progressive, she has pledged to “launch tools in which you can see our progress, our successes, and our failures in real time.”

In that vein, she has said she will introduce public monitoring of the police department to ensure that it follows the city’s edicts against using local officers to conduct federal immigration enforcement.

She will also publicly audit spending on homelessness, a priority for Ms. Bass, who used city funds for motel rooms to address rampant street encampments after the pandemic. Ms. Raman’s plan is to use time-limited housing vouchers, which are less expensive but depend on a steady supply of vacant apartments and willing landlords.

She has also indicated that she will lean into her training as an urban planner, just as Ms. Bass leaned into hers as a physician assistant and lawmaker. To create urgency around the city’s chronic maintenance issues, Ms. Raman has pledged to publicly map broken streetlights and publish deadlines to repair them. To hasten building, she said, she will put housing permits on a “shot clock” to cut red tape.

Mike Murphy, a Republican political consultant who has advised past mayoral candidates in Los Angeles, said that Ms. Raman will have her work cut out for her. Aside from financial constraints, she will be working with a City Council whose members all declined to endorse her, though they congratulated her at a council meeting last week.

“She’s going to need a big coalition to make any changes, because politically in L.A., they’re so hard,” said Mr. Murphy. “Will she start firing police chiefs and be a justice warrior? Or will she widen her appeal so she can actually do things? D.S.A., not D.S.A.? It’s an open question. But it’s time for action now.”

item.title: Judge Could Set New Trial Date for Lindsay Clancy
item.description:
A judge could set a new trial date as soon as Monday for Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts woman whose first trial for the deaths of her three young children ended with a deadlocked jury.

Prosecutors have not yet said whether they plan to retry Ms. Clancy on first-degree murder charges, lesser charges or at all. But Judge William Sullivan indicated at a hearing earlier this month that he intends to choose a tentative start date for a second trial, and that he may do so at a 10 a.m. hearing on Monday in Plymouth Superior Court.

Jurors at Ms. Clancy’s first trial were unable to break their 11-1 deadlock after nearly 40 hours of deliberations, and the judge declared a mistrial on Sept. 2. If prosecutors reduce the charges to second-degree murder or manslaughter, Ms. Clancy could avoid a second jury trial and have her fate decided by a judge instead.

Judge Sullivan dismissed several motions by Ms. Clancy’s lawyers last week, including one that argued for the dismissal of the charges. Her lawyers have asserted that any retrial would constitute double jeopardy because the mistrial could have been avoided if the judge had dug deeper into the conduct of the lone juror who voted to convict.

The defense team said in its motion that if the judge had investigated further, he might have found grounds for dismissing that juror and replacing him with an alternate.

In his ruling, Judge Sullivan found that such an inquiry would have been “impermissibly coercive,” given the lack of evidence that the juror had done anything wrong. Judge Sullivan also dismissed a defense motion arguing for further investigation of the holdout juror.

Kevin Reddington, the lawyer for Ms. Clancy, had argued that the juror had failed to disclose information about his own past criminal charges. Heather O’Connor, a lawyer for the juror, has said that he “believed he was truthful” on the juror questionnaire that he filled out during the jury selection process last summer.

Ms. Clancy, 36, has remained in custody at a state hospital since the mistrial. Her trial was televised and lasted for six weeks, attracting an enormous and opinionated audience.

Mr. Reddington had argued during the trial that she was not criminally responsible for killing Cora, 5; Dawson, 3; and Callan, 8 months, because she was experiencing severe postpartum mental illness and hallucinated a voice that ordered her to kill them and herself. After strangling her children, Ms. Clancy cut her wrists and throat and jumped from a window, sustaining spinal injuries that left her paralyzed.

The trial revived a national debate about postpartum mental illness, its treatment and how resulting criminal cases should be treated by the courts. Ms. Clancy’s lawyer focused on her persistent but unsuccessful efforts to find effective mental health care in the months before the killings.

The online furor around the case, and the intense scrutiny and criticism of the jurors after the mistrial, have raised concerns about the prospect of seating another jury for a second trial, given the likely trepidation of prospective jurors.

At the hearing on Nov. 2, Mr. Reddington expressed impatience with prosecutors after they declined to say whether they would try Ms. Clancy again for first-degree murder. Timothy Cruz, the Plymouth district attorney, has pledged to continue seeking justice for the Clancy children, and he is widely seen as an uncompromising prosecutor.

“The ball is in Mr. Cruz’s court,” Mr. Reddington said at the hearing this month.

item.title: ‘Steering Failure’ Likely Caused Tanker’s Collision With Riverboat, N.T.S.B. Says
item.description:
The tanker that struck a docked riverboat carrying nearly 200 people on Friday in New Orleans appeared to have had a “steering failure,” according to initial findings from the National Transportation Safety Board.

It was not immediately clear what that meant or what may have caused it, officials said, emphasizing that the findings were preliminary.

“We purposefully worded it in that way,” Bart Barnum, a senior marine engineer in the N.T.S.B.’s Office of Marine Safety, said during a news conference on Sunday. “It can be many different things. That is something we are investigating very closely.”

Because of “an issue with the steering on board,” Mr. Barnum said, the tanker’s rudder remained in a starboard position, which caused it to veer toward the east bank of the Mississippi River.

Investigators also said they were analyzing the tanker’s voyage data recorder but were not ready to publicly release its information, including the vessel’s speed at the time of the collision.

The tanker, named the Atlantic Asphalt, lost control on Friday and veered into the side of the passenger boat, causing it to capsize at its dock on the river. The crash prompted a wide-scale search-and-rescue operation that ended with all passengers and crew members accounted for, in what Gov. Jeff Landry of Louisiana called “a literal miracle on the Mississippi.”

The American Cruise Lines riverboat, named American Heritage, took about 22 minutes to capsize, John DeLeeuw, a member of the N.T.S.B., said at the news conference on Sunday.

The tanker had 19 crew members and a local pilot on board, Mr. DeLeeuw said. The riverboat had 140 passengers and 50 crew members on board at the time of the crash.

Officials said 32 people were taken to the hospital and one had serious injuries. People clung to the rails and screamed as the riverboat overturned, videos posted online showed.

The riverboat, which had arrived from Natchez, Miss., had been docked for about two hours and was beginning to unload passengers when the tanker struck it, said Kimberly Curth, a spokeswoman for the Port of New Orleans.

item.title: Trump Administration Moves to Close A.I. Chip Loophole Ahead of China Trip
item.description:
The Trump administration said on Monday that it was moving forward with a new rule that would clamp down on China’s ability to access advanced A.I. chips through the use of data centers outside China’s borders.

The rule aims to close what many in Washington see as a loophole that has allowed China to sidestep a Commerce Department ban that prevents Chinese firms from buying the most advanced A.I. chips made by companies like Nvidia. China’s ability to continue accessing the chips by renting them from data centers in Southeast Asian countries and elsewhere has been a focus of contention within the Trump administration.

The new rule establishes restrictions for overseas data centers that supply “significant volumes of computing power” to firms with headquarters in a small group of high-risk countries, a list that includes China, Russia and Iran. Data centers are also required to perform due diligence on those customers. The provision will “undermine” the ability of companies in those countries from using U.S. chips to train advanced A.I. models, the release said.

It will also require a license to export advanced chips to companies with headquarters in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand or Brazil, which have a higher than normal risk of smuggling, the administration said.

A plan to restrict that loophole comes just days before President Trump is scheduled to travel to China for an economic summit, where he will also meet with the Chinese leader, Xi Jinping.

The formerly obscure issue has become more prominent in recent weeks with the revelations about Megaspeed, a Singaporean data center firm created by a woman who had an affair with Jensen Huang, who was ousted as Nvidia’s chief executive last week. U.S. authorities deemed the woman, Alice Huang, to be an asset for Chinese intelligence services, and they are investigating Megaspeed over allegations of smuggling chips to China.

Megaspeed’s business, the operation of data centers in Southeast Asia that remotely serve Chinese clients, is legal. That means Chinese companies that are blocked from buying advanced Nvidia chips directly can simply rent them through other Southeast Asian firms.

Nvidia and its proponents contend that the sales help create jobs in the United States and ensure that companies around the world are reliant on American technology.

But some officials in the Trump administration and in Congress increasingly appear to believe that Chinese access to these data centers has undercut U.S. export controls and allowed China’s artificial intelligence ecosystem to flourish. Some worry this could give Beijing an economic edge, as well as a military one.

In a news release, the Commerce Department said the rule was “designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries.”

The move would bring America’s rules on remote access of data centers into alignment with its rules on the physical shipment of sensitive American technology, the department said.

Just before leaving office, the Biden administration issued global rules on chip sales, including restrictions on Chinese firms remotely accessing data centers. Trump officials said they would no longer enforce the rules after Mr. Trump won another term, and in May 2025 they officially rescinded the restrictions.

Since then, various draft versions of the rules have gained momentum in the government, only to be shot down by opponents.

In recent months, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and the U.S. trade representative, Jamieson Greer, have all pushed to reinstate broad restrictions on data centers, amid concerns about Nvidia’s advanced chips reaching China.

But they faced pushback from Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who oversees chip export policy. Mr. Lutnick has pushed for a leaner version of the rules, one that would be less onerous for Nvidia and foreign data centers.

The announcement published Monday said that the new rule was “written by and at the direction of the Department of Treasury and the National Security Council” — both parts of the administration that have pushed for more stringent rules.

It remains to be seen whether the new rules will trigger blowback from China. Mr. Trump heads to Asia this week and arrives in China on Wednesday for meetings that are expected to address the war in Iran, nuclear nonproliferation and trade.

In a telephone briefing on Friday, a senior administration official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity as part of the ground rules of the call, said the administration had been discussing potential measures on remote access and did not expect countermeasures from China in response. The moves would close loopholes in existing measures to counteract both smuggling and remote access of data centers, and the Chinese have stated publicly that they are not involved with smuggling, the official said.

Another senior administration official on the call said the situation with Nvidia would not have any bearing on the trip. Export controls are national security matters and are not up for negotiation with the Chinese, the official said.

]]>

item.title: Trump Says He’s Open to Reinstatement of Jensen Huang as Nvidia Chief
item.description:
President Trump said on Monday that he was open to seeing Jensen Huang reinstated as the head of Nvidia, his latest public expression of support for the executive who resigned after admitting to an affair with a woman whom U.S. officials had identified as a Chinese intelligence asset.

“I would not mind; I would not mind that,” Mr. Trump told reporters on the South Lawn of the White House as he departed for a dayslong trip to Asia, including a stop in China.

“I think he learned a big lesson — I guess maybe one lesson is more important than another,” he added.

The president cast doubt on whether Alice Huang, the woman with whom Mr. Huang had a relationship, was actually a spy.

“I don’t know that she is a spy,” Mr. Trump said. “Usually, what happens with that is that any woman coming to the country that’s a beautiful woman that comes from China, they say she’s a spy. I don’t know that she was a spy at all.”

The president has repeatedly defended Mr. Huang since the revelations.

Last week, Mr. Trump called Mr. Huang before he stepped down and urged him to keep fighting for his job, The New York Times reported.

Mr. Trump was warned at least twice about Mr. Huang’s relationship with Ms. Huang, who intelligence agencies concluded had been recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security, The Times has reported. The first warning was late last year, and the second was in the spring.

But the president has continued to express sympathy for Mr. Huang. He told reporters last week that he was concerned with how the technology executive was holding up amid the controversy.

“I did speak to him today just to see if he’s feeling all right,” Mr. Trump said then, adding: “I believe he’s suffering greatly. I read his statement, and I believe he’s suffering greatly. More so because of his family, his wife who he loves and his family, but he is definitely suffering.”

item.title: Person Detained in Illinois Bomb Case, Authorities Say
item.description:
A person was in custody on Monday morning in connection with a bomb threat that led to a lengthy evacuation in Peoria, Ill., the city’s police department said.

Semone Roth, a Peoria police spokeswoman, did not name the person and declined to provide additional information. She said updates would come from the F.B.I.

F.B.I. officials in Springfield, Ill., said on Monday that they were “conducting law enforcement activity in Peoria County” in connection with the case but did not provide any information on arrests. “The investigation remains ongoing,” the F.B.I. statement said.

Officials found and deactivated a bomb on Friday at the BioUrja Renewables ethanol plant south of downtown Peoria, leading to a lengthy evacuation order for people within a one-mile radius of the facility. While emergency crews searched the plant for more explosives, events were canceled, roads were blocked, and some residents took shelter in the basement of a high school.

The search for additional bombs ended on Saturday afternoon without any being located, and residents were allowed to return home. No injuries were reported.

This is a developing story. Check back for updates.

Devlin Barrett contributed reporting.
